rules.statement: Route every server-initiated outbound HTTP fetch of a client- or user-supplied URL through a dedicated named HttpClient whose ConnectCallback applies the shared SSRF guard, pins the socket to the validated resolved IP, and disables automatic redirects.
rules.why: Fetching a client-supplied URL is a textbook SSRF sink. One fetch had used a plain unnamed HttpClient that followed redirects with no SSRF control, which left a confused-deputy gap.
rules.check: Look for new code that fetches a URL taken from client metadata, a request parameter or registration data using an unnamed or plain HttpClient, an HttpClient without the SSRF-guard ConnectCallback, or a handler with AllowAutoRedirect left enabled.

rules.statement: Do not add any configuration option, flag or allow-list that re-permits private, loopback, link-local, CGNAT, unique-local, multicast, reserved or other IANA special-use addresses in the outbound SSRF guard; extension points may only block more addresses.
rules.why: The special-use address floor is a fact, not a deployment opinion. Re-permitting any of it is an SSRF footgun, and no knob may weaken a security control below its safe baseline.
rules.check: Flag options or filter logic that can allow an address the hardcoded floor blocks. Also flag filter-composition logic that blocks an address only when all checks agree; it should block when the floor or any filter blocks.

rules.statement: Bound every outbound fetch of a client-supplied URL: require an absolute https URI, apply a wall-clock timeout and a response-size cap, and honor an optional host allow-list.
rules.why: Without these limits, a client-controlled URL can hang the server, exhaust its memory, or reach unintended hosts.
rules.check: Look for outbound fetches of client-supplied URLs that accept http or relative URIs, have no timeout, read the full body without a size limit, or ignore the configured allowed-hosts setting.

rules.statement: When a per-client setting overrides a server-wide security limit, treat it only as a tighter ceiling: intersect allow-lists, and take the minimum of numeric limits such as timeouts, size caps and cache durations.
rules.why: These per-client settings are ceilings. A client must never loosen the server's limits.
rules.check: Look for code that merges per-client and server settings so that the client value simply replaces the server value, or that takes the maximum or union where a limit could be loosened.

rules.statement: When fetching a remote client key set (jwks_uri) fails because it is unreachable, oversized, disallowed or malformed, log a warning and fail closed by using only the locally known keys; never throw out of the resolver and never grant access.
rules.why: A missing key set should simply make signature verification fail. A fetch error must not turn into an exception path or an authentication bypass.
rules.check: Look for key-resolution code that propagates fetch exceptions, returns a permissive result, or skips signature verification when the remote fetch fails.

rules.statement: When importing a fetched JWK Set, skip any JWK with an unsupported kty or malformed key material instead of failing the whole set.
rules.why: One bad key should never break a key set that is otherwise usable.
rules.check: Look for JWK Set import loops that throw or return failure for the whole set when a single key cannot be parsed or has an unsupported kty.

rules.statement: Convert runtime-fetched JWKs into key objects through the existing shared secret import and serialization pipeline, not with new RSA/EC parsing code.
rules.why: Reusing the pipeline keeps parsing, validation and the key-type taxonomy consistent with inline key import.
rules.check: Look for new code that parses JWK RSA or EC parameters directly with RSA.ImportParameters, ECDsa.ImportParameters or similar instead of calling the shared importer.

rules.statement: Code that verifies a client-signed JWT, such as client_assertion or a JAR request object, must get the client's verification keys from the key-resolver service, not read the client's stored keys directly.
rules.why: Reading stored keys directly ignores keys the client publishes at jwks_uri, so assertions signed with those keys can never validate.
rules.check: Look for client-assertion or request-object validation code that reads the client's stored secret-key collection directly instead of calling the key resolver.

rules.statement: Register replaceable public extension seams with TryAddSingleton, and register additive multi-implementation extension points with TryAddEnumerable, so that deployments can override or extend them.
rules.why: Seams like the key resolver and the address filters are meant to be overridable or extensible through DI.
rules.check: Look for public seam registrations that use AddSingleton, which prevents overriding, or multi-implementation extension points registered in a way that replaces or duplicates implementations.

rules.statement: Cache a successfully fetched remote key set per URI with an absolute expiration bounded by the configured cache duration.
rules.why: Caching keeps verification from fetching on every request, and the bound still lets clients rotate keys.
rules.check: Look for jwks_uri-style fetches made on every validation with no cache, or caches without an absolute expiration or not keyed by URI.
